notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: How does SAFe define Agile Architecture?
notes.back: A set of values, practices, and collaborations that support the active, evolutionary design and architecture of a system. It avoids Big Design Up Front (BDUF) but still gives enough intentional guidance to keep large systems coherent.
notes.source: FW: Agile Architecture · ASR: 'Agile Architecture' chapter

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: Agile Architecture balances which two complementary approaches?
notes.back: Emergent design (bottom-up, from teams, one increment at a time) and intentional architecture (planned, cross-team, purposeful guidance). Together they pave the Architectural Runway.
notes.source: FW: Agile Architecture; Architectural Runway · ASR: 'Agile Architecture'

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: Define emergent design.
notes.back: Defining and extending the architecture only as necessary to deliver the next increment of functionality. Grounded in Agile Manifesto principle 11: 'the best architectures, requirements, and designs emerge from self-organizing teams.' Risks at scale: duplicated effort, inconsistency, poor Nonfunctional Requirements (NFR) performance.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: Define intentional architecture.
notes.back: A set of purposeful, planned architectural initiatives that enhance solution design, performance, and usability and provide guidance for cross-team design and implementation synchronization. Owned mainly by System/Solution/Enterprise Architects, delivered through Enablers.
notes.source: FW: Agile Architecture · SD: 'Enterprise Solution Delivery' chapter

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: Define the Architectural Runway.
notes.back: The existing code, components, and technical infrastructure needed to implement near-term features with minimal redesign and delay. It enables continuous flow through the Continuous Delivery Pipeline (CDP) and lets the technology landscape evolve with business needs.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: How is the Architectural Runway built and why must it be continuously extended?
notes.back: Built by implementing Enablers (epics → capabilities → features → stories). Features consume runway as they are delivered, so architects must keep investing (typically via capacity allocation) or the runway shrinks and feature velocity drops.
notes.source: FW: Architectural Runway; Enablers · ARCH Part 1/4

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: List the principles of Agile Architecture in the SAFe 6.0 article.
notes.back:
• Design emerges. Architecture is a collaboration.
  • The bigger the system, the longer the runway.
  • Build the simplest architecture that can possibly work.
  • When in doubt, code or model it out.
  • They build it, they test it.
  • There is no monopoly on innovation.
  • Implement architectural flow.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: Leffingwell's original eight principles of Agile Architecture (Agile Software Requirements) — which two are worded differently from the SAFe 6.0 list?
notes.back: The ASR list adds/words two explicitly: 'The teams that code the system design the system' and 'System architecture is a role collaboration'. The rest match the SAFe list (simplest architecture, when in doubt code it out, they build it they test it, bigger system longer runway, no monopoly on innovation, implement architectural flow).
notes.source: ASR: 'Agile Architecture' chapter (Part IV, Portfolio) · SSA

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: Which development practices does Agile Architecture support, according to the SAFe 6.0 article?
notes.back:
• Collaboration
  • Design simplicity
  • Balancing intentional and emergent design
  • Designing for testability, deployability, and releasability
  • Rapid prototyping
  • Domain modeling
  • Decentralized innovation

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: Name the three architect roles in SAFe and their scope.
notes.back:
• Enterprise Architect — Portfolio level; technology strategy, enabler epics, cross-value-stream alignment.
  • Solution Architect — Large Solution level; Solution Train, Solution Intent, capabilities.
  • System Architect — Essential level; one Agile Release Train (ART), features, ART runway.
notes.source: FW: Enterprise Architect; Solution Architect; System Architect · SD: 'SAFe Roles'

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: Who forms the leadership 'trio' of an Agile Release Train (ART), and what is the architect's part in it?
notes.back: Product Management (what), Release Train Engineer (RTE) (how the train runs), System Architect (how it is built). The architect owns the architecture vision, enabler definition, NFRs, and technical guidance across the ART's teams.
notes.source: FW: System Architect; Agile Release Train · scaledagile.com ARCH course page

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: What is the equivalent leadership trio on a Solution Train?
notes.back: Solution Management, Solution Train Engineer (STE), and Solution Architect.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: What are the three dimensions of Lean-Agile Leadership an architect must exemplify?
notes.back:
• Leading by example (authenticity, emotional intelligence, lifelong learning, growing others, decentralized decision-making)
  • Mindset and principles (Lean-Agile mindset, SAFe core values, SAFe principles)
  • Leading change
notes.source: FW: Lean-Agile Leadership · SD: 'Lean-Agile Leadership' chapter · ARCH Part 1

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: What two bodies of knowledge make up the Lean-Agile Mindset in SAFe?
notes.back: The House of Lean (goal: value; pillars: respect for people and culture, flow, innovation, relentless improvement; foundation: leadership) and the Agile Manifesto (4 values, 12 principles).
notes.source: FW: Lean-Agile Mindset · SD: 'Lean-Agile Mindset' chapter

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: List the 10 SAFe principles (SAFe 6.0).
notes.back:
1. Take an economic view
  2. Apply systems thinking
  3. Assume variability; preserve options
  4. Build incrementally with fast, integrated learning cycles
  5. Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems
  6. Make value flow without interruptions
  7. Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning
  8. Unlock the intrinsic motivation of knowledge workers
  9. Decentralize decision-making
  10. Organize around value
notes.source: FW: SAFe Principles · SD: 'SAFe Principles' chapter

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: How does an architect apply Principle #3 — Assume variability; preserve options?
notes.back: Keep multiple design/requirement options open (Set-Based Design), model or prototype alternatives, and converge at the last responsible moment based on objective evidence rather than committing to a single point solution early.
notes.source: FW: SAFe Principle #3; Set-Based Design · ASR

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: Principle #9 — which decisions should an architect centralize and which decentralize?
notes.back: Centralize: infrequent, long-lasting, significant economies of scale (e.g., technology standards, platform choice, security baselines). Decentralize: frequent, time-critical, requiring local information (e.g., component design, implementation details) — push to teams.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: Principle #1 — what five variables does the SAFe economic framework ask you to trade off?
notes.back: Lead time (cycle time), product cost, development expense, risk, and value. Architectural choices are evaluated on total economics, not local technical elegance; use Cost of Delay (CoD) to sequence work.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: Principle #6 — name the eight flow accelerators (SAFe 6.0).
notes.back:
1. Visualize and limit Work In Process (WIP)
  2. Address bottlenecks
  3. Minimize handoffs and dependencies
  4. Get faster feedback
  5. Work in smaller batches
  6. Reduce queue lengths
  7. Optimize time 'in the zone'
  8. Remediate legacy policies and practices
Architecture affects #3, #4, #5 directly (decoupling, testability, deployability).
notes.source: FW: SAFe Principle #6 (Make value flow without interruptions)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::01 Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
notes.front: Principle #10 — why does 'Organize around value' matter for architecture?
notes.back: Team/ART structure and system structure mirror each other (Conway's law). Architects should shape solution boundaries so that value streams and ARTs can deliver independently, reducing cross-train dependencies.
notes.source: FW: SAFe Principle #10; Development Value Streams

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::02 Architecting for DevOps and Release on Demand
notes.front: What does the DevOps acronym CALMR stand for?
notes.back: Culture of shared responsibility, Automation of the Continuous Delivery Pipeline, Lean flow, Measurement of everything, Recovery (fast recovery, rollback, fix-forward).
notes.source: FW: DevOps · SD: 'Agile Product Delivery' chapter

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::02 Architecting for DevOps and Release on Demand
notes.front: Name the four aspects of the Continuous Delivery Pipeline (CDP).
notes.back: Continuous Exploration (CE), Continuous Integration (CI), Continuous Deployment (CD), Release on Demand (RoD).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::02 Architecting for DevOps and Release on Demand
notes.front: What are the four activities of Continuous Exploration (CE), and which one is the architect's home turf?
notes.back: Hypothesize → Collaborate & Research → Architect → Synthesize. The Architect activity: design for continuous delivery, evolve the runway, define enablers and NFRs, and decide what to build vs. buy.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::02 Architecting for DevOps and Release on Demand
notes.front: What are the four activities of Continuous Integration (CI)?
notes.back: Develop → Build → Test end-to-end → Stage. Architectural enablers: trunk-based development, test automation, integration environments, decoupled components.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::02 Architecting for DevOps and Release on Demand
notes.front: What are the four activities of Continuous Deployment (CD)?
notes.back: Deploy → Verify → Monitor → Respond. Architect for infrastructure-as-code, telemetry, and fast rollback/recovery.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::02 Architecting for DevOps and Release on Demand
notes.front: What are the four activities of Release on Demand (RoD)?
notes.back: Release → Stabilize & Operate → Measure → Learn. Key architectural idea: the business decides when to release, independent of deployment.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::02 Architecting for DevOps and Release on Demand
notes.front: Why and how should architecture decouple deployment from release?
notes.back: So that code can be deployed continuously while value is released when the business chooses. Techniques: feature toggles, dark launches, canary releases, blue/green deployments, decoupled release elements (release components on their own cadence).
notes.source: FW: Release on Demand; Agile Architecture

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::02 Architecting for DevOps and Release on Demand
notes.front: What does 'architecting for testability' involve?
notes.back: Modular, loosely coupled components with clear interfaces; dependency injection and test doubles; observable state; automated test hooks at every level (unit, component, system, NFR). Supports 'they build it, they test it'.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::02 Architecting for DevOps and Release on Demand
notes.front: What does 'architecting for deployability' involve?
notes.back: Infrastructure as code, immutable/versioned environments, small independently deployable units, backward-compatible interfaces and data migrations, automated configuration, and telemetry so deployments can be verified.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::02 Architecting for DevOps and Release on Demand
notes.front: What is the architect's responsibility toward the System Team and pipeline automation?
notes.back: Define the target pipeline architecture, ensure the solution is built so it can be automated (build, test, deploy), collaborate with the System Team on integration environments, and champion the DevOps culture — architects participate in executing the CDP, not only designing it.
notes.source: FW: System Team; DevOps · ARCH Part 2

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::02 Architecting for DevOps and Release on Demand
notes.front: Name the six flow metrics in SAFe 6.0.
notes.back: Flow distribution, flow velocity, flow time, flow load, flow efficiency, flow predictability. Architects watch distribution (share of enablers/debt) and flow time (impact of architectural bottlenecks).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::02 Architecting for DevOps and Release on Demand
notes.front: What are the five dimensions of Built-In Quality in SAFe 6.0?
notes.back: Business functions, software applications, IT operations, hardware, cyber-physical systems. Common foundations: flow, architecture & design quality, code quality, system quality, release quality.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::03 Aligning Architecture with Business Value
notes.front: What is the Portfolio Vision?
notes.back: A description of the future state of a portfolio's value streams and solutions, and how they will cooperate to achieve the enterprise's objectives and strategic themes. It is a primary input to solution visions and to enabler epics.
notes.source: FW: Portfolio Vision · SD: 'Lean Portfolio Management' chapter

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::03 Aligning Architecture with Business Value
notes.front: What does the Portfolio Canvas capture, and why should an architect read it?
notes.back: Value propositions, customer segments, channels, customer relationships, the portfolio's value streams and solutions, key partners/activities/resources, budgets, revenue streams, cost structure, and KPIs. Architects use it to see which solutions and value streams their technology strategy must serve.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::03 Aligning Architecture with Business Value
notes.front: What are Strategic Themes and how are they expressed in SAFe 6.0?
notes.back: Differentiating business objectives that connect the portfolio to enterprise strategy. In SAFe 6.0 they are expressed as Objectives and Key Results (OKRs). They influence the portfolio vision, budgets, backlog prioritization, solution visions, and roadmaps.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::03 Aligning Architecture with Business Value
notes.front: How do strategic themes flow into architectural decisions?
notes.back: Strategic themes → portfolio vision/canvas → technology strategy (Enterprise Architect) → enabler epics in the Portfolio Kanban → solution/architecture vision → enabler capabilities/features in Solution Train/ART backlogs → Architectural Runway.
notes.source: FW: Strategic Themes; Enterprise Architect; Enablers · ARCH Part 3/7

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::03 Aligning Architecture with Business Value
notes.front: Distinguish operational and development value streams.
notes.back: Operational value streams deliver products/services to customers (e.g., process a loan). Development value streams build the solutions that operational value streams use. ARTs are organized around development value streams.
notes.source: FW: Value Streams; Development Value Streams · SD: 'Organizational Agility'

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::03 Aligning Architecture with Business Value
notes.front: What does Value Stream Mapping measure, and how does it point to architecture work?
notes.back: For each step: process time, delay/wait time, and percent complete and accurate (%C&A); total flow time and flow efficiency. Long delays in integration/test/deploy steps often signal architectural constraints that enablers must remove.
notes.source: FW: Value Stream Mapping (Continuous Delivery Pipeline)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::03 Aligning Architecture with Business Value
notes.front: What is an Agile Release Train (ART)?
notes.back: A long-lived, cross-functional team of Agile teams (typically 50–125 people) that plans, commits, develops, and delivers solutions together on a common cadence (the Planning Interval, PI), organized around a development value stream.
notes.source: FW: Agile Release Train · SD: 'Agile Product Delivery'

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::03 Aligning Architecture with Business Value
notes.front: What is a Solution Train and when is it needed?
notes.back: The organizational construct that coordinates multiple ARTs (and suppliers) building a large, complex solution (systems of systems, often with compliance needs). Uses Solution Intent, capabilities, Pre-/Post-PI Planning, and Solution Demo.
notes.source: FW: Solution Train · SD: 'Enterprise Solution Delivery'

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::03 Aligning Architecture with Business Value
notes.front: What are Value Stream KPIs?
notes.back: Quantifiable measures of how a value stream is performing against its intended business outcomes (e.g., revenue, cost, customer satisfaction, flow metrics). Used by Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) to govern value streams instead of governing projects.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::03 Aligning Architecture with Business Value
notes.front: How do Agile architects 'support business alignment' per the SAFe 6.0 article?
notes.back: By optimizing the architecture to support the value stream end-to-end — the architecture must accelerate (not impede) frequent, independent releases that let the business meet its objectives.
notes.source: FW: Agile Architecture (Architecture enables business value)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: What is the Solution Vision and who owns it?
notes.back: A description of the future state of the solution: customer needs, features/capabilities, NFRs, and how it fits the solution context. Owned by Product/Solution Management; architects contribute the technical direction and the architecture vision.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: Define Solution Intent.
notes.back: The repository for storing, managing, and communicating the knowledge of current and intended solution behavior: specifications, designs, and tests; current state and future state; fixed and variable intent. Essential for large solutions and regulated environments.
notes.source: FW: Solution Intent · SD: 'Enterprise Solution Delivery'

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: Distinguish fixed and variable Solution Intent.
notes.back: Fixed: known, non-negotiable elements (regulatory constraints, chosen standards, decisions already made). Variable: elements still open, explored via Set-Based Design and closed as knowledge grows. Over time variable intent becomes fixed.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: What is Solution Context?
notes.back: The operational environment in which the solution is deployed and used: interfaces to other systems, deployment/hosting environment, regulations, usage constraints. It constrains the architecture and is co-owned with the customer/operations.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: Explain Set-Based Design (SBD) and its economic rationale.
notes.back: Keep multiple requirement and design options open, eliminate weaker ones as objective data arrives, and commit at the last responsible moment. Reduces the risk of early point solutions being wrong; supports Principle #3.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: What role does Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) play in SAFe?
notes.back: Models (rather than documents) become the primary artifacts of Solution Intent: they capture requirements, design, and analysis, are versioned like code, support simulation/early validation, and generate documentation as needed.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: Order the SAFe work-item hierarchy from portfolio to team.
notes.back: Epic (portfolio) → Capability (large solution) → Feature (ART) → Story (team). Each level has a business and an enabler variant.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: Name the four types of Enablers.
notes.back: Exploration (research/prototyping to learn), Architectural (build the runway), Infrastructure (environments, pipeline, tooling), Compliance (regulatory/verification work). They exist at every backlog level.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: What are Nonfunctional Requirements (NFRs) and where do they live in SAFe?
notes.back: System qualities and constraints ('-ilities': security, performance, reliability, maintainability, compliance…). They are persistent constraints on the backlogs (not backlog items themselves), captured in Solution Intent, and verified continuously via the System Team/automated tests.
notes.source: FW: Nonfunctional Requirements · ASR: 'Nonfunctional Requirements' chapter

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: What characteristics should a well-written NFR have?
notes.back: Bounded (has a context/threshold), Independent, Negotiable (economic trade-off known), Testable (objective measure). Avoid 'the system shall be fast'.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: How does SAFe treat compliance and the Lean Quality Management System (QMS)?
notes.back: Build compliance into the flow: define a Lean QMS (policies, practices, roles), capture continuous objective evidence (versioned models, automated tests, traceability in Solution Intent), release on cadence with audits happening on working systems rather than end-phase documentation.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: What are the three roadmap horizons in SAFe, and what do architects contribute?
notes.back: PI roadmap (current committed PI + ~2 forecast PIs), Solution roadmap (longer-range, milestone-based), Portfolio roadmap (epics across value streams over time). Architects add and sequence enablers so runway lands before the features that consume it.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: Rule of thumb for sequencing runway work on the roadmap?
notes.back: Architectural enablers should be planned roughly one PI ahead of the features that depend on them, so teams find the runway in place rather than blocked by it.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::04 Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
notes.front: What is capacity allocation and who negotiates it?
notes.back: A per-PI agreement on how much ART/Solution Train capacity goes to business features vs. enablers/technical debt vs. maintenance. Negotiated between Product/Solution Management and the System/Solution Architect; prevents the runway from being starved.
notes.source: FW: ART and Solution Train Backlogs (capacity allocation)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::05 Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
notes.front: What is PI Planning and how long is a Planning Interval (PI)?
notes.back: The cadence-based, face-to-face (or distributed) event where all ART teams plan the next PI together, aligning to a shared mission and vision. A PI is typically 8–12 weeks (commonly 4 development iterations + 1 Innovation and Planning (IP) iteration); the event itself is 2 days.
notes.source: FW: PI Planning; Planning Interval · SD: 'Agile Product Delivery'

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::05 Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
notes.front: Which briefings open Day 1 of PI Planning, and which one belongs to the architect?
notes.back: Business context (Business Owner/executive), Product/Solution vision (Product Management), Architecture vision and development practices (System Architect), Planning context (RTE).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::05 Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
notes.front: What should the architecture vision briefing contain?
notes.back: Enabler features planned for the PI, changes to the runway, new NFRs or constraints, development practice expectations (e.g., CI, test automation, definition of done), and technical dependencies/interfaces the teams must respect.
notes.source: FW: PI Planning; System Architect · ARCH Part 5/9

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::05 Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
notes.front: What does the architect do during team breakouts?
notes.back: Circulate between teams: clarify enablers and NFRs, help resolve design questions, identify cross-team dependencies and interface risks early, and steer toward the simplest architecture — without dictating team-level design.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::05 Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
notes.front: What happens in the Management Review and Problem-Solving session, and why is the architect there?
notes.back: End of Day 1: management (Business Owners, PM, RTE, architects) reviews draft plans, adjusts scope, resolves dependencies/resource conflicts, and makes decisions overnight. The architect judges technical feasibility, sequencing of enablers, and whether to descope features lacking runway.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::05 Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
notes.front: What does ROAM stand for?
notes.back: Program risks are Resolved, Owned, Accepted, or Mitigated during PI Planning Day 2. Architectural risks (unproven technology, integration) are commonly Owned by the architect or Mitigated via exploration enablers.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::05 Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
notes.front: How does the confidence vote work?
notes.back: Each team, then the whole ART, votes 1–5 (fist of five) on confidence in meeting PI objectives. Average below 3 → rework the plan; anyone voting 1 or 2 must explain. Consistent low votes on technical items are a signal of missing runway.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::05 Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
notes.front: Distinguish committed and uncommitted PI objectives.
notes.back: Committed objectives are those the team is confident in; uncommitted objectives are planned but carry more uncertainty (they still count in the plan, not in the commitment). Business Owners assign business value (1–10) to each — including enabler objectives.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::05 Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
notes.front: What is shown on the ART Planning Board (formerly Program Board)?
notes.back: Features per team per iteration, cross-team dependencies (red strings), and milestones/events. Architects use it to verify that enablers precede the features that consume them.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::05 Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
notes.front: What is Pre-PI Planning (Solution Train)?
notes.back: Held before ART PI Planning events: Solution Train stakeholders align on the solution vision, solution roadmap, capabilities, and solution-level PI objectives so each ART plans within shared intent. The Solution Architect presents the solution architecture vision.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::05 Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
notes.front: What is Post-PI Planning (Solution Train)?
notes.back: After the ARTs' PI Planning: ARTs present plans, cross-ART dependencies and risks are ROAMed at solution level, solution PI objectives are finalized, and a solution-level confidence vote is taken.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::05 Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
notes.front: State the Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF) formula.
notes.back: WSJF = Cost of Delay (CoD) ÷ Job Size (duration). Higher WSJF is done first. Used for ART/Solution Train backlogs (features/capabilities) and for the Portfolio Backlog (epics).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::05 Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
notes.front: What are the three components of Cost of Delay (CoD) in WSJF?
notes.back: User-business value + Time criticality + Risk reduction and/or opportunity enablement (RR/OE). Enablers typically score high on RR/OE — that is how architects argue for runway economically rather than 'because it's the right thing'.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::06 Supporting Continuous Delivery During PI Execution
notes.front: Distinguish Iteration Review, System Demo, and Solution Demo.
notes.back: Iteration Review: team-level, each iteration. System Demo: integrated ART-level increment, every iteration (the primary objective measure of ART progress — Principle #5). Solution Demo: integrated Solution Train increment, at least once per PI.
notes.source: FW: System Demo; Solution Demo; Iteration Review

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::06 Supporting Continuous Delivery During PI Execution
notes.front: What are the three parts of Inspect & Adapt (I&A)?
notes.back:
1. PI System Demo
  2. Quantitative and qualitative measurement
  3. Retrospective and problem-solving workshop (root-cause analysis, e.g., fishbone/5 Whys → improvement backlog items)
Architects bring data on flow, quality, and runway health.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::06 Supporting Continuous Delivery During PI Execution
notes.front: What is the ART Sync?
notes.back: The combined Coach Sync (Scrum Masters/Team Coaches + RTE: progress, impediments) and PO Sync (Product Owners + PM: scope, priorities). Architects attend to surface technical dependencies and runway status.
notes.source: FW: ART Sync (Coach Sync, PO Sync)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::06 Supporting Continuous Delivery During PI Execution
notes.front: What coordination events exist at the Solution Train level?
notes.back: Solution Train Sync (STE-led coordination across ARTs), plus an architect sync among System Architects led by the Solution Architect to keep architecture, interfaces, and Solution Intent aligned.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::06 Supporting Continuous Delivery During PI Execution
notes.front: What is the Innovation and Planning (IP) iteration used for?
notes.back: Estimating buffer, innovation/hackathons, infrastructure and tooling work, continuing education, and hosting I&A and next PI Planning. Architects often use it for exploration enablers and runway spikes — but it must not become the default place for overflow.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::06 Supporting Continuous Delivery During PI Execution
notes.front: Summarize the architect's responsibilities during PI execution.
notes.back: Guide implementation of enabler features; review designs/interfaces; make sure NFRs are being tested continuously; manage technical debt; prepare for system/solution demos; attend ART Sync; track runway consumption and adjust the next PI's enablers.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: Define Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and its three dimensions.
notes.back: The competency that aligns strategy and execution by applying Lean and systems thinking to strategy and investment funding, Agile portfolio operations, and governance. Dimensions: Strategy and Investment Funding, Agile Portfolio Operations, Lean Governance.
notes.source: FW: Lean Portfolio Management · SD: 'Lean Portfolio Management' chapter

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: What are the activities of Strategy and Investment Funding?
notes.back: Connect the portfolio to enterprise strategy; maintain the portfolio vision; realize the vision through epics; establish Lean budgets and guardrails; establish portfolio flow. The Enterprise Architect co-develops strategic themes and the technology portion of the vision.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: What are the activities of Agile Portfolio Operations?
notes.back: Coordinate value streams; support ART/Solution Train execution; foster operational excellence. Enabled by the Agile Program Management Office (APMO), Lean-Agile Center of Excellence (LACE), RTE/STE Communities of Practice, and the Portfolio Sync.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: What are the activities of Lean Governance?
notes.back: Forecast and budget dynamically; measure portfolio performance (Value Stream KPIs, flow, Measure and Grow); coordinate continuous compliance. The Enterprise Architect helps ensure technology decisions stay within guardrails and compliance needs.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: Who are the core participants in the LPM function?
notes.back: Enterprise executives (strategy, funding), Business Owners (accountable for value stream outcomes), and Enterprise Architects (technology strategy) — supported by Epic Owners, APMO/LACE, and Value Stream/ART leadership (RTEs, Product/Solution Management).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: Summarize the Enterprise Architect's responsibilities in SAFe 6.0.
notes.back:
• Participate in portfolio strategy (strategic themes, portfolio vision/canvas)
  • Guide enterprise technology strategy and standards (build/buy/reuse, platforms, cloud, data, AI)
  • Define and steward enabler epics through the Portfolio Kanban (often as Epic Owner)
  • Promote adaptive design/engineering practices and DevOps across ARTs
  • Facilitate reuse of ideas, components, patterns
  • Align Solution and System Architects across value streams
notes.source: FW: Enterprise Architect · SD: 'Lean Portfolio Management'

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: What does an Epic Owner do?
notes.back: Coordinates a portfolio epic through the Portfolio Kanban: defines the epic hypothesis, MVP, and Lean Business Case with stakeholders; presents it to LPM for a go/no-go; after approval, works with Product/Solution Management and ARTs to decompose it into capabilities/features, tracks the MVP hypothesis, and reports back to LPM. It is a temporary responsibility, not a full-time job.
notes.source: FW: Epic Owners · SD: 'Lean Portfolio Management'

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: Who typically acts as Epic Owner for enabler epics, and what is the hardest part of that job?
notes.back: The Enterprise Architect (or a Solution/System Architect). Hardest part: expressing architectural value in business terms (Cost of Delay, risk reduction, opportunity enablement, flow improvement) so LPM can compare it with business epics.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: Define a portfolio Epic and its two types.
notes.back: A significant solution development initiative whose size/cost exceeds the LPM-defined threshold and therefore needs analysis, an MVP, a Lean Business Case, and LPM approval. Types: Business epics (customer/business value) and Enabler epics (architecture, infrastructure, exploration, compliance). Smaller epics can also live at Solution Train/ART level.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: Give the structure of the Epic Hypothesis Statement.
notes.back: For [customers] who [do something], the [solution] is a [something – the 'how'] that [provides this value]; unlike [competitor/current state], our solution [does this better]. Plus: business outcomes hypothesis, leading indicators, NFRs.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: What does a Lean Business Case contain?
notes.back: Epic description and hypothesis; MVP definition and full-scope description; business outcomes and leading indicators; NFRs; cost forecast for MVP and full implementation (initially T-shirt sizes); in-house vs. outsourced; sequencing, dependencies, and impacted ARTs/value streams.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: What is an MVP in the SAFe epic sense?
notes.back: A Minimum Viable Product: the smallest increment that can test the epic hypothesis with real users/data. After the MVP the leading indicators decide: persevere (continue via normal backlog flow) or pivot/stop. For enabler epics the 'MVP' is often a thin vertical slice of the new architecture in production.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: List the states of the Portfolio Kanban.
notes.back: Funnel → Reviewing (epic hypothesis statement, rough WSJF) → Analyzing (Lean Business Case, MVP, WIP-limited) → Portfolio Backlog (approved, prioritized by WSJF) → Implementing (MVP, then persevere/pivot) → Done.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: Trace an enabler epic from idea to Architectural Runway, naming the roles at each step.
notes.back: Enterprise Architect identifies the need from technology strategy → enters Funnel → EA (as Epic Owner) writes the hypothesis statement (Reviewing) → Lean Business Case + MVP with Solution/System Architects and Business Owners (Analyzing) → LPM go/no-go → Portfolio Backlog (WSJF) → Solution/System Architects decompose into enabler capabilities/features (Implementing) → runway extended → EA reports outcomes to LPM (Done).
notes.source: FW: Portfolio Kanban; Enterprise Architect; Epic Owners · ARCH Part 7

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: What are Lean Budgets and how do they differ from project funding?
notes.back: Funding is allocated to development value streams (long-lived ARTs) rather than to individual projects; value streams decide how to spend within guardrails. Architecturally this means stable teams own systems for their lifetime — no project-end handoffs, and technical debt has an owner.
notes.source: FW: Lean Budgets · SD: 'Lean Portfolio Management'

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: Name the four Lean Budget Guardrails.
notes.back:
1. Guiding investments by horizon
  2. Applying capacity allocation to optimize value and solution integrity
  3. Approving significant initiatives (epics over the threshold go through LPM)
  4. Continuous Business Owner engagement
Guardrails 2 and 3 are where the architect's runway investment is protected and reviewed.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: Describe the investment horizons used in guardrail 1.
notes.back: Horizon 3 — Evaluating (exploration, prototypes); Horizon 2 — Emerging (new solutions growing); Horizon 1 — Investing / Extracting (current core solutions); Horizon 0 — Retiring (decommissioning). Enterprise Architects advise on when a technology moves between horizons.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: Name the three main LPM events and their cadence.
notes.back: Strategic Portfolio Review (quarterly-ish: strategy, vision, budgets, KPIs), Portfolio Sync (more frequent, e.g., monthly: epic progress, impediments, KPIs), Participatory Budgeting (per PI or twice a year: adjust value stream budgets).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: What is Participatory Budgeting (PB) and what does the architect bring?
notes.back: A collaborative event where LPM stakeholders allocate the portfolio budget across value streams and significant epics using real cost estimates. The Enterprise Architect brings cost/feasibility forecasts for enabler epics and argues their Cost of Delay.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: What is the Portfolio Backlog and the Portfolio Roadmap?
notes.back: Portfolio Backlog: the holding area for approved business and enabler epics awaiting implementation capacity, ordered by WSJF. Portfolio Roadmap: a multi-year view of planned epics/milestones across value streams — the Enterprise Architect ensures enabler epics are sequenced before dependent business epics.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: What is the architect's contribution when the enterprise identifies or expands value streams?
notes.back: In the Value Stream and ART Identification workshop: map systems to operational value streams, identify shared platforms and reuse, assess technical feasibility and dependencies of new development value streams, and propose ART boundaries that minimize cross-train coupling.
notes.source: FW: Value Stream and ART Identification (Implementation Roadmap) · ARCH Part 7

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: How do architects collaborate across value streams?
notes.back: Via the Enterprise Architect's cross-portfolio view, architecture Communities of Practice (CoPs), Shared Services/platform teams, common technology standards and guardrails, and shared enabler epics that serve several value streams.
notes.source: FW: Communities of Practice; Shared Services; Enterprise Architect

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: How do Business Owners and architects interact?
notes.back: Business Owners assign business value to PI objectives (including enabler objectives), attend PI Planning and management review, and are accountable for value stream outcomes; architects must explain enablers in outcome terms so Business Owners rate them fairly and keep engaging (guardrail 4).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::07 Lean Portfolio Management (LPM) and the Architect
notes.front: What is the Agile Program Management Office (APMO)?
notes.back: The evolved PMO that supports LPM: sponsors and supports ART/Solution Train execution, coordinates value streams, fosters operational excellence, and often runs the LACE together with the Enterprise Architect on technology-strategy topics.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::08 Leading as an Architect During a Lean-Agile Transformation
notes.front: List Kotter's 8 steps for leading change as used in SAFe.
notes.back:
1. Establish a sense of urgency
  2. Create a powerful guiding coalition
  3. Develop the vision and strategy
  4. Communicate the vision
  5. Empower employees for broad-based action
  6. Generate short-term wins
  7. Consolidate gains and produce more change
  8. Anchor new approaches in the culture
notes.source: FW: Lean-Agile Leadership (Leading change) · SD: 'Lean-Agile Leadership'

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::08 Leading as an Architect During a Lean-Agile Transformation
notes.front: Name the steps of the SAFe Implementation Roadmap.
notes.back: Reach the tipping point → Train Lean-Agile change agents → Train executives, managers, leaders → Create a Lean-Agile Center of Excellence (LACE) → Identify value streams and ARTs → Create the implementation plan → Prepare for ART launch → Train teams and launch the ART → Coach ART execution → Launch more ARTs and value streams → Extend to the portfolio → Accelerate.
notes.source: FW: Implementation Roadmap · SD: 'Implementation Roadmap' chapter

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::08 Leading as an Architect During a Lean-Agile Transformation
notes.front: What is the Lean-Agile Center of Excellence (LACE) and why should architects join it?
notes.back: A small team dedicated to implementing the SAFe Lean-Agile way of working. Architects in the LACE make sure the transformation addresses technical agility: DevOps pipeline, architecture for continuous delivery, and enabler funding — not only process and roles.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::08 Leading as an Architect During a Lean-Agile Transformation
notes.front: How does the architect's role change from traditional to Lean-Agile architecture?
notes.back: From approver/gatekeeper producing up-front documents to collaborator and coach: shares decisions with teams (Principle #9), validates architecture with working systems (Principle #5), invests in runway incrementally, and leads by example in engineering practices.
notes.source: FW: Agile Architecture; Lean-Agile Leadership · ARCH Part 8

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::08 Leading as an Architect During a Lean-Agile Transformation
notes.front: What should an architect's personal action plan after the ARCH course typically contain?
notes.back: Concrete steps for: adopting Agile Architecture practices on your ART/Solution Train, contributing enablers to backlogs, improving the CDP, engaging with LPM/Enterprise Architecture on enabler epics, and specific behaviors to model as a Lean-Agile leader.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::09 Preparing Architecture for PI Planning
notes.front: Distinguish the Portfolio, Solution Train, and ART backlogs.
notes.back: Portfolio Backlog: approved epics (LPM). Solution Train Backlog: capabilities and enablers (Solution Management + Solution Architect). ART Backlog: features and enablers for one ART (Product Management + System Architect). Each is prioritized with WSJF.
notes.source: FW: Portfolio Backlog; ART and Solution Train Backlogs

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::09 Preparing Architecture for PI Planning
notes.front: What is the standard Feature format, and how do enabler features differ?
notes.back: Name + benefit hypothesis + acceptance criteria; sized to fit in one PI for one ART. Enabler features use the same format, but the benefit hypothesis states the technical/flow outcome (e.g., 'deployment time ↓ from 4h to 20min') so it can be prioritized alongside business features.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::09 Preparing Architecture for PI Planning
notes.front: What is the architect's role in ART backlog refinement before PI Planning?
notes.back: Write and refine enabler features; ensure business features have needed runway or an accompanying enabler; add NFR-related acceptance criteria; estimate job size for WSJF; agree capacity allocation with Product Management; produce the architecture vision briefing.
notes.source: FW: ART and Solution Train Backlogs; System Architect · ARCH Part 9

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::09 Preparing Architecture for PI Planning
notes.front: Architect's pre-PI-Planning checklist (top items).
notes.back:
• Top-10 features have runway or paired enablers
  • Enabler features written with benefit hypothesis + acceptance criteria
  • WSJF scored with Product Management
  • NFR changes documented in Solution Intent
  • Architecture vision & development practices briefing ready
  • Known cross-team/cross-ART dependencies pre-identified
  • Capacity allocation agreed

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::10 Bridge — Architecture ↔ Portfolio Roles
notes.front: Map each SAFe architect to the portfolio artifact/role they primarily work with.
notes.back:
• Enterprise Architect ↔ LPM, Strategic Themes, Portfolio Vision/Canvas, Enabler Epics, Portfolio Kanban, Guardrails
  • Solution Architect ↔ Epic Owners (decomposing epics into capabilities), Solution Intent, Solution Roadmap
  • System Architect ↔ Product Management & Business Owners (features, PI objectives), ART Backlog, PI Roadmap

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::10 Bridge — Architecture ↔ Portfolio Roles
notes.front: How does value-stream funding (Lean Budgets) change the economics of Architectural Runway compared with project funding?
notes.back: With project funding, runway is nobody's budget line and gets cut. With Lean Budgets, the value stream owns its systems long-term, so runway and technical-debt work are funded through capacity allocation inside the value stream budget (guardrail 2) and, for large items, as enabler epics approved by LPM (guardrail 3).
notes.source: FW: Lean Budgets; Guardrails; Architectural Runway

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::10 Bridge — Architecture ↔ Portfolio Roles
notes.front: An enabler epic is estimated above the LPM threshold. Which roles are involved in the go/no-go and what evidence is expected?
notes.back: Epic Owner (usually the Enterprise Architect) presents the Lean Business Case with MVP, cost forecast, leading indicators, and WSJF inputs; Business Owners and enterprise executives in LPM decide; Solution/System Architects supply feasibility and sizing; the APMO tracks it on the Portfolio Kanban.
notes.source: FW: Epics; Portfolio Kanban; LPM roles

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::10 Bridge — Architecture ↔ Portfolio Roles
notes.front: Which portfolio-level measures should an Enterprise Architect report on?
notes.back: Flow metrics for value streams (distribution of enabler work, flow time), Value Stream KPIs, progress of enabler epics against leading indicators, technical-debt/runway health, and DevOps/CDP maturity (Measure and Grow assessments).
notes.source: FW: Metrics; Measure and Grow; Value Stream KPIs

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::10 Bridge — Architecture ↔ Portfolio Roles
notes.front: Strategic Themes are expressed as OKRs. How should an architect translate a theme like 'reduce time-to-market by 50%' into portfolio work?
notes.back: Identify the architectural constraints on flow (e.g., monolithic release coupling, manual environments) → propose enabler epics (e.g., decoupled deployment, pipeline automation) with a hypothesis tied to the OKR's key result → add them to the Portfolio Kanban → sequence on the portfolio roadmap ahead of the business epics that need them.
notes.source: FW: Strategic Themes; OKRs; Enablers; Portfolio Kanban

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::10 Bridge — Architecture ↔ Portfolio Roles
notes.front: Which LPM event is the right place to raise: (a) an urgent cross-value-stream technical impediment, (b) a proposal to retire a legacy platform, (c) re-allocating budget toward a platform enabler?
notes.back: (a) Portfolio Sync; (b) Strategic Portfolio Review (investment horizon 0 — retiring); (c) Participatory Budgeting.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::00 Exam and Reference
notes.front: Official facts about the SAFe for Architects (ARCH) certification (SAFe 6.0).
notes.back: 3-day instructor-led course (advanced level); timed, multiple-choice, 45-question exam with a coaching report; unlimited practice test; certification renewed yearly. Target: system, solution, and enterprise architects, senior technical leaders, SPCs.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::00 Exam and Reference
notes.front: The nine parts of the SAFe for Architects course (as published by training partners).
notes.back:
1. Exemplifying Lean-Agile Architecture
  2. Architecting for DevOps and Release on Demand
  3. Aligning Architecture with Business Value
  4. Developing Solution Vision, Solution Intent, and Roadmaps
  5. Coordinating Architecture Throughout PI Planning
  6. Supporting Continuous Delivery During PI Execution
  7. Supporting New Strategic Themes and Value Streams
  8. Leading as an Architect During a Lean-Agile Transformation
  9. Preparing Architecture for PI Planning
notes.source: ARCH course outline (training-partner syllabus pages, SAFe 6.0)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects (ARCH 6.0)::00 Exam and Reference
notes.front: Which books back this deck, and what does each cover best?
notes.back:
• SAFe 5.0 Distilled (Knaster & Leffingwell, 2020): competencies incl. LPM and Enterprise Solution Delivery, principles, roles. (Latest print 'Distilled'; 6.0 changes are on the framework site.)
  • Agile Software Requirements (Leffingwell, 2011): original Agile Architecture principles, runway, NFRs, epics/portfolio planning.
  • Scaling Software Agility (Leffingwell, 2007): origins of intentional architecture and the runway concept.
  • SAFe 4.5 Reference Guide (Leffingwell et al., 2018): article-by-article reference (dated versions of terms).
notes.source: Book metadata verified via publisher/O'Reilly listings
